title: Cache Tag Invalidation in ASP.NET Core
description: Learn how to implement tag-based cache invalidation to evict groups of related cache entries efficiently when underlying data changes.

data.text: Caching solves the read problem, but invalidation is the real challenge. When a product price changes, every cached page, list, and snippet that contains that product becomes stale. Naive approaches — removing individual cache keys or waiting for TTL — are error-prone and slow. Tag-based invalidation solves this by grouping cache entries under named tags so you can evict all related entries with a single operation.

ASP.NET Core does not ship with built-in tag-based invalidation, but the pattern is straightforward: store a reverse index (tag to keys) in Redis, and when data changes, look up the affected keys and remove them.

terms.definition: A strategy that groups cache entries by logical tags and evicts all entries sharing a tag in a single operation.
A Redis Set that stores the list of cache keys associated with a specific tag. Used to look up keys for bulk deletion.
A surge of requests that hit a cold cache simultaneously after invalidation, overwhelming the data source.
A strategy that serves expired cache data while refreshing it in the background, preventing stampedes.

data.text: The implementation has three parts: the tag helper that adds tags when setting cache entries, the reverse-index maintenance that tracks which keys belong to each tag, and the invalidation method that reads the index and removes the entries.

data.title: Tag-Aware Cache Helper
data.content: A small helper class wraps IDistributedCache and maintains tag indexes in Redis Sets.

data.title: Key Design Choice: Atomic Tag Assignment
data.text: Always add the key to each tag Set in the same operation that writes the cache entry. If you write the cache first and add tags later, a crash in between will leave an orphaned entry with no tag index — it will never be invalidated.

When an update event fires — for example, a product price is changed in the database — the application calls InvalidateByTagAsync with the product category tag. The method reads all keys stored under that tag from Redis and removes them in parallel. The tag index Set is then deleted to free up Redis memory.

data.caption: Tag-based cache invalidation sequence
data.definition:
sequenceDiagram
    participant App as Application
    participant Cache as Redis Cache
    participant TagIdx as Tag Index (Redis Set)
    App->>Cache: Set(key=products:123, value=..., tags=[category:electronics])
    Cache-->>TagIdx: SADD tag:category:electronics products:123
    Note over App,TagIdx: Later: product price changes
    App->>TagIdx: SMEMBERS tag:category:electronics
    TagIdx-->>App: [products:123, products:456, ...]
    App->>Cache: DEL products:123, products:456, ...
    App->>TagIdx: DEL tag:category:electronics

data.text: If a tag contains thousands of keys, deleting them all synchronously can block the Redis server. Use SCAN instead of SMEMBERS for large sets, and delete keys in batches using Redis pipelining. For very large datasets, consider sharding tag indexes across multiple Redis keys.

data.title: Invalidation Anti-Patterns to Avoid
items: Invalidating by partial key match with KEYS — it blocks Redis in production
Using a single catch-all tag that accumulates all keys over time
Forgetting to remove keys from the tag Set after deletion, causing memory leaks
Relying on TTL alone when you need immediate consistency after writes

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Tag-based invalidation groups related cache entries under named tags
Redis Sets are ideal for storing the tag-to-keys reverse index
Always add keys to tag Sets atomically with the cache write operation
Batch deletions for large tag sets to avoid blocking Redis
Clear the tag index Set after invalidation to prevent memory leaks
data.takeaway: Tag-based invalidation keeps cached data consistent after writes without relying solely on TTL expiration.
